## Chapter Summary

Accounting data in modern organizations is stored in relational databases, which organize information into tables connected by defined relationships. Understanding this structure is a prerequisite for writing SQL queries, building Power BI data models, and preparing data for analysis in Excel. The relational model, first proposed by Codd (1970), has become the standard approach to data storage in business information systems and underlies virtually every ERP system and accounting software package in use today.

A relational database consists of tables, each storing information about one type of entity or event. Tables are organized into rows (one per instance) and columns (one per attribute), and every column has a data type that determines what values it can hold and what operations are possible. How a database stores those types depends on the system: the Charles River SQLite file stores numbers as INTEGER or REAL, and stores text and dates as TEXT. Primary keys uniquely identify each row in a table, and foreign keys create connections between tables by referencing the primary key of a related table. These keys formalize the cross-references that have always existed in accounting records: a sales invoice references a customer, a general ledger entry references an account, and an order line references a product.

A database can enforce these relationships through constraints, but it does not have to. The Charles River database enforces its primary keys and the uniqueness of many document numbers, while its foreign keys are logical relationships that the data follows but the file does not enforce. That is why analysts test referential integrity rather than assume it, and why the relationships must be defined by hand when the data is loaded into a tool such as Power BI.

Relationships between tables have a cardinality that specifies how many rows on each side of the relationship can be associated, and an optionality that specifies whether a row must participate at all. One-to-many relationships are the most common in accounting data: one customer has many orders, one account has many GL entries, one item appears on many order lines. One-to-one relationships appear when a later stage of a process has its own table, such as a work order and its close record. Many-to-many relationships are resolved through junction tables, such as the Charles River SalesOrderLine table that connects SalesOrder to Item and the CashReceiptApplication table that connects receipts to invoices. Understanding cardinality is essential for avoiding analytical errors such as double-counting when combining data from multiple tables.

Entity-Relationship diagrams provide a visual map of a database's structure. They show tables as labeled rectangles, relationships as connecting lines, and cardinality and optionality through crow's foot notation. Reading an ER diagram is a practical skill that auditors, analysts, and accountants use when planning data extractions, designing queries, and building data models. The Charles River ER diagrams and the table-group comparison in this chapter illustrate how table group complexity scales with business process complexity, from the small Master Data group to the large Order-to-Cash group, while the underlying relational principles remain constant.

The familiar structures of accounting, including the chart of accounts, the general ledger, and the sub-ledgers, map directly to tables and relationships in the Charles River database. The chart of accounts is the Account table with a self-referencing hierarchy through ParentAccountID. The general ledger is the GLEntry table, linked to the chart of accounts through AccountID. Sub-ledgers are the transactional cycle tables, such as SalesInvoice and PurchaseInvoice, that connect to GLEntry through the source-document columns SourceDocumentType, SourceDocumentID, and SourceLineID, a logical link that can point to a different table for every posting. Cross-group bridge keys such as ItemID, AccountID, and EmployeeID tie the entire database together, making it possible to perform financial reporting, audit testing, and managerial analysis directly from the database, which is exactly what you will do in the chapters ahead.
